chunks: Drive circuit for a high-side NFET. The question: Design a circuit to properly drive a high-side NFET. Why is it needed?
A high-side NFET needs its gate about 10 volts above its source, and its source rides up to the motor supply. So you need a small gate supply that moves with the switch node.
The usual answer is a bootstrap: a diode and a capacitor beside a gate-driver chip.
The capacitor charges while the low side is on, then floats up with the switch node and powers the gate drive.
Fill a bucket at ground level, then carry it up in an elevator to the 24th floor.
The water still stands the same height above the bucket's floor, even though the bucket is now high above the ground.
The capacitor is the bucket, and the 10 volts charge is the water. A one-way valve (the diode) stops the water draining back down.
The bucket slowly leaks, so it cannot stay up there forever without a refill.
With a fixed gate rail, V GS drops linearly as the source rises and the FET turns itself off before the source gets to 7 volts. A bootstrapped supply holds V GS near 9.
6 volts for any V SW .
Switch node (SW): the junction between the high-side and low-side FETs, where the motor connects.
Bootstrap capacitor ( C boot ): the capacitor between the driver's boot pin and SW that holds the floating gate supply.
Bootstrap diode: lets current charge the capacitor, and blocks it when SW rises. Gate charge ( Q g ): the charge needed to turn the FET fully on.
Charge pump: a circuit that makes a supply above the rail, so the FET can stay on 100% of the time.
Use a 24 volts bridge, a 10 volts driver supply and a FET with Q g equals 40 nC. While the low side is on, SW is near 0 volts, so the capacitor charges through a 0.
4 volts diode to about 9. 6 volts. When SW jumps to 24 volts, the boot pin sits near 33. 6 volts and the gate gets its 9. 6 volts. To keep the voltage from sagging more than 0.
5 volts, the capacitor needs at least 40 nC over 0. 5 volts equals 80 nanofarads, so use about 470 nanofarads. That is the whole idea.
"A high-side NFET needs its gate about 10 volts above its source, and the source is the switch node, so I need a gate supply that floats with it.
I'd use a half-bridge driver with a bootstrap: a fast diode from the 10 volts supply to a capacitor that sits between the boot pin and the switch node.
It charges when the low side is on and lifts the gate drive when the high side turns on. Size it as gate charge over allowed droop, about 0.
5 microfarads for 40 nC, add a gate resistor and a gate-source pull-down, and use a charge pump if I need 100% duty."
